definition: Data mining, the process of discovering patterns in large data sets, has been used in many applications.
details: Data mining, the process of discovering patterns in large data sets, has been used in many applications.

explainer.lead: Data mining is used to find useful patterns in large collections of data, from groups of similar records to relationships between events. Its value comes from turning raw records into clues that people can investigate and use.

tiers.eli5: Imagine looking through thousands of shopping receipts and noticing that certain items often appear together. Data mining is like doing that search with a computer: it looks through lots of records for patterns that would be hard to spot one receipt at a time. The pattern can be helpful, but people still need to check whether it makes sense.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners apply data mining after collecting and cleaning relevant records, then search for patterns such as associations, clusters, or trends. Results should be checked on data not used to discover them, because large data sets can contain many accidental patterns. A useful finding also needs enough context to support a sensible action rather than being treated as proof of cause and effect.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a data set D, data mining seeks patterns or models whose structure and quality can be evaluated with a chosen criterion, rather than merely returning individual records. The discovered pattern is a candidate regularity in D, not automatically a causal law or a guarantee about new data. Important limits include spurious patterns, sensitivity to data preparation, and reduced reliability when findings are not validated beyond the discovery data.

explainer.example: Suppose a shop examines thousands of anonymized transactions and finds that bread and butter appear together unusually often. That association could prompt a closer look at shopping habits, although it does not explain by itself why customers buy the items together.

usedIn.name: Retail analysis
usedIn.detail: Transaction records can be examined for products that are frequently bought together.

usedIn.name: Customer analysis
usedIn.detail: Large collections of customer records can be searched for recurring groups or behaviours.

usedIn.name: Operations analysis
usedIn.detail: Operational records can be examined for repeated sequences or unusual combinations of events.

explainer.intuition: A large data set can hide regularities that are invisible when records are viewed individually. Data mining searches across those records to surface patterns worth examining.
howItWorks: Gather records that describe the activity being studied.
Clean and organize the records so they can be compared.
Search for recurring relationships, groups, or sequences.
Evaluate which patterns are consistent and potentially useful.
Interpret the findings before using them to guide a decision.
explainer.whyItMatters: Data mining can make large data sets more useful by revealing patterns that people might otherwise miss. Careful evaluation helps separate promising findings from coincidences.
misconceptions: A discovered pattern does not necessarily show that one event causes another.
Data mining is not simply searching for one known record; it looks for broader patterns.
Finding a pattern in existing data does not guarantee that it will hold in new data.

diagram.caption: Data mining turns prepared records into candidate patterns, which still require evaluation.
